patches.old: \paragraph{Non-uniqueness.} Not uniquely. Shifting the right half of a well sideways changes the shape without changing $\Phi$, because only the \emph{width} of the allowed region at each height enters $\Phi$.
patches.new: \paragraph{Non-uniqueness.} Not uniquely. For a single well with minimum $V_{\min}$, let $x_L(V)<x_R(V)$ be the two turning points at height $V$ and $w(V)=x_R(V)-x_L(V)$ the width. Changing variable from $x$ to $V$ separately on the two sides of the minimum (exactly as in Step~1 below) gives $\Phi(E)=\int_{V_{\min}}^{E}\sqrt{E-V}\,\bigl[x_R'(V)-x_L'(V)\bigr]\dd V=\int_{V_{\min}}^{E}\sqrt{E-V}\,w'(V)\,\dd V$. So $\Phi$ depends only on the width at each height. Sliding each horizontal slice of the well sideways by an amount that depends on height (a shear, which keeps $w(V)$ fixed) changes the shape without changing $\Phi$. Example: $V=\abs x$ has $w=2V$; the lopsided well $V=-2x$ for $x<0$, $V=\tfrac23x$ for $x>0$ has $x_L=-V/2$, $x_R=3V/2$, so also $w=2V$, and both have $\Phi=\tfrac43E^{3/2}$.
